👉 Please do not open PRs which fix all errors at once, or even all errors in one error-specific baseline, unless there are just a few. Conversely, avoid opening a PR to just fix a single error out of many, unless it is justified. Try to keep PRs organized by component or by file. PRs can be opened referencing this Trac ticket, avoiding the need to open a ticket for these ongoing improvements. summary: Administration: Replace Dashicons icon font with @wordpress/icons SVG components in wp-admin
_description:
== Problem / Current Behavior ==

The WordPress admin area (wp-admin) still relies on Dashicons, an icon font introduced in WordPress 3.8 (released December 12, 2013 — over 12 years ago). While Dashicons served WordPress well, the icon font approach has significant limitations:

 * '''Inconsistency''': The block editor and Site Editor already use `@wordpress/icons` (SVG-based React components), while the rest of wp-admin uses the legacy Dashicons font. This creates a visual and technical split within the same application.
 * '''Performance''': The entire icon font (~300+ glyphs) is loaded, regardless of how many icons a page actually uses. This adds unnecessary weight to every admin page load.
 * '''Accessibility''':
   * '''Screen readers''': Icons may be read as nonsense or ignored entirely, confusing users who rely on assistive technology.
   * '''Font overrides''': Users who change fonts for readability can break all icons, turning them into empty squares.
   * '''Copy-paste''': Copying text that includes icons produces random, meaningless characters.
   * '''High-contrast mode''': Icons can vanish when users enable high-contrast or forced-colors settings in their OS.
   * '''No built-in meaning''': Icon fonts are just styled characters with no inherent description — accessibility has to be added manually.5.5. No new icons can be added.

== Proposed Enhancement ==

Replace Dashicons icon font usage in wp-admin with `@wordpress/icons` SVG components (or inline SVGs derived from the same library). This would:

 1. Unify the icon system across all of WordPress, block editor, Site Editor, and classic admin screens would all use the same modern icon library.
 2. Enable tree-shaking so that only the icons actually used on a given page are loaded.
 3. Improve accessibility: inline SVGs support `aria-label` for example.
 4. Allow new icons to be added as needed without growing a monolithic font file.


== Rationale ==

This is not a new idea, it has been the stated direction of the WordPress project since 2020:

 * The [https://make.wordpress.org/design/2020/04/20/next-steps-for-dashicons/ Make/Design blog post] (April 2020) confirmed Dashicons was closed to new requests and that future efforts would focus on the new Icon component.
 * [ticket:49913] explicitly states: "This update is the final planned update of the Dashicons font. Moving forward, the more modern approach of using SVG icons directly (as the block editor currently does) will be explored."
 * [ticket:47498] comments reference "a long standing plan to remove all font icons from core in favor of SVGs."

Six years have passed since this direction was set, and no formal ticket tracks the actual migration work. This ticket aims to formalize the effort and track progress.

== Backward Compatibility ==

This is a critical consideration. Many plugins and themes use `dashicons-*` CSS classes for admin menus, meta boxes, and custom UI. A migration plan should:

 * Maintain the `dashicons` stylesheet as a deprecated fallback for a defined transition period (multiple major releases).
 * Provide a compatibility layer so that existing `dashicons-*` class references continue to render correctly, perhaps by mapping them to their SVG equivalents.
 * Document the migration path for plugin and theme developers with clear timelines.

== Related Tickets / References ==

 * [ticket:49913] — Final Dashicons update (WordPress 5.5)
 * [ticket:47498] — Checkbox/radio SVG migration, discusses removing font icons from Core
 * [ticket:41074] — Dashicons 4.9–5.2, discusses SVG direction for the admin
 * [https://make.wordpress.org/design/2020/04/20/next-steps-for-dashicons/ Next steps for Dashicons] — Make/Design official post
 * [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/07/15/dashicons-in-wordpress-5-5-the-final-update/ Dashicons in WordPress 5.5: The Final Update] — Dev note
 * [https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/tree/trunk/packages/icons @wordpress/icons package on GitHub]

summary: Host Test Results show the database version as Unknown for core's PHPUnit runs
_description:
The core PHPUnit runs that report to the Host Test Results show the database version as Unknown, for example https://make.wordpress.org/hosting/test-results/r64355/wpdevbot-r64355-8-5-unknown/.

Since https://github.com/WordPress/phpunit-test-runner/pull/319, the test runner gets the version from the database server with `SELECT VERSION()`. In a report-only run like core's, `report.php` does this through `get_env_details()`, which needs `WPT_DB_HOST`, `WPT_DB_USER`, `WPT_DB_PASSWORD` and `WPT_DB_NAME`. The "Submit test results" step in `reusable-phpunit-tests-v3.yml` passes none of them, so the version comes back empty.

The fix is to pass the values the test suite already uses in the local Docker environment (`mysql`, `root`, `password`, `wordpress_develop_tests`, as set in `tools/local-env/scripts/install.js`).

I tested the exact report command against the local Docker environment, with the upload sent to a local endpoint instead of WordPress.org. With MySQL 8.4 the version goes from empty to `8.4.11`, and with MySQL 9.7 to `9.7.2`. Nothing else in the uploaded data changes, and the credentials are not part of it.

Related: https://github.com/WordPress/phpunit-test-runner/issues/135

summary: Update counts in the folded admin menu don't refresh after updating a plugin
_description:
When the admin menu is folded, the update count next to "Plugins" doesn't change after you update a plugin on the page. It keeps the old number until you reload.

The admin menu prints each top-level item's update count twice: once in the menu link, and once in the submenu header (`.wp-submenu-head`). The submenu header is what shows when the menu is folded, either after clicking "Collapse Menu" or automatically on screens between 783 and 960 pixels wide. `wp.updates.refreshCount()` only updates the copy in the menu link, so the folded menu never changes.

=== Steps to reproduce
1. Have two plugins with updates available.
2. Make the browser window about 900 pixels wide, or click "Collapse Menu".
3. Go to "Plugins > Installed Plugins" and click "update now" for one of them.
4. Hover over "Plugins" in the admin menu.

Expected: the count shows 1.

Actual: it still shows 2. After updating both plugins it still shows 2 instead of no count.

The same thing happens with the "Themes" count in the network admin, which is also a top-level menu item. On a single site the theme count is on the "Themes" submenu item, so it isn't affected.

=== Environment
- WordPress: 7.2-alpha (trunk)
- Browser: Chromium 149
- Single site and multisite

I have a patch ready and will link the PR here.

summary: KSES: Re-implement using HTML API
_description:
Since its initial commit, WordPress has relied on the KSES library to sanitize and normalize and transform content from untrusted sources. Unfortunately, the parsing inside of `wp_kses()` has never been spec-compliant, leading to numerous challenges in safely, efficiently, and reliably fulfilling its purpose.

The HTML API provides a mechanism for structurally interacting with HTML in an efficient manner, and `wp_kses()` should be rewritten to lean on that existing capability.

== Resolves

 - #25851 Large attribute values may crash PCRE patterns and cause content loss.
 - #37698 Global pollution in `wp_kses_split()` calls.
 - #48873 CSS contents are corrupted by `wp_kses()`.
 - #51482 `wp_kses()` turns SCRIPT and STYLE content into renderable text.
 - #52333 `wp_kses()` and HTML disagree on the set of named character references.
 - #58377 Block names with consecutive hyphens are corrupted.
 - #58921 Valid tag names are rejected from the allow-list.
 - #59310 `parse_blocks()` called unnecessarily.
 - #61246 `wp_kses()` un-comments HTML comments.
 - #62024 `wp_kses_post()` incorrectly escapes “<” in attribute values.

=== Potentially resolves

 - #51093 CSS `>` corruption.
 - #56118 Slashes are improperly stripped when exporting data.

== Related

 - #63881 Deprecate `wp_kses_stripslashes()`.
 - #65599 HTML sanitization API implementation.

Fix duplicate <h1> landmark tags on login and password recovery pages
_description:
### Description
An accessibility (a11y) and markup validation issue exists on the core login, forgot password, and registration screens (`wp-login.php`). The page currently generates two separate `<h1>` heading landmarks simultaneously, which violates semantical HTML standards and disrupts document structure for screen reader users.

### Root Cause Analysis
In `src/wp-login.php`, an `<h1>` tag with the class `.screen-reader-text` is dynamically outputted to act as an accessible text heading representing the active page title (e.g., "Log In"). However, directly below that landmark block, the presentation layout wraps the visible WordPress website branding logo image anchor (`.wp-login-logo`) within a second, nested `<h1>` element. 

### Proposed Fix
The brand presentation element does not require header hierarchical value. This patch replaces the outer wrapper around the logo anchor link from an `<h1>` element to a fallback semantic block `<div>` tag with `role="presentation"`. 

This safely reduces the heading layer footprint back to a clean, single `<h1>` per view, allowing screen readers to seamlessly announce the actual utility context of the page title without configuration conflicts.

### Environment Details
- **Affected File:** `src/wp-login.php`
- **Testing Setup:** Local WP (Flywheel dev stack)
- **Repository Branch Target:** trunk / core develop clone

summary: Notes: Restore child notes trashed along with their parent note
_description:
Gutenberg PR: https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/84100

When a top-level note is trashed, `wp_trash_comment()` also trashes its child notes. However, `wp_untrash_comment()` has no counterpart for this: when the parent note is restored, its child notes stay in the trash.

To fix this, `wp_untrash_comment()` needs a counterpart to the child-trashing logic in `wp_trash_comment()`. The approach can follow the precedent of [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/2bf0714531e2d478640ccb46fe5463a092530ac4/src/wp-includes/post.php#L4351-L4356 wp_trash_post_comments()] / [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/2bf0714531e2d478640ccb46fe5463a092530ac4/src/wp-includes/post.php#L4412-L4429 wp_untrash_post_comments()]:

* When a top-level note is trashed, store the IDs of the child notes that are not yet in the trash (i.e. the ones being trashed along with the parent) in the parent note's `_wp_trash_meta_children` meta.
* When the parent note is untrashed, restore only the recorded child notes that are still in the trash, then delete the meta.

Importantly, a child note the user trashed individually before trashing the parent should **not** be restored when the parent is trashed and then restored. The parent's trash/untrash cycle should only undo what it did itself.

summary: Many PHPUnit tests are not well isolated
_description:
In talking about tests at WCUS 2026, we reminded ourselves that many of our PHPUnit tests leak state and/or depend on previously leaked state. This is easy to see by running the tests in an arbitrary order:

{{{
npm run test:php -- --order-by=random
}}}

This lack of isolation can result in varied problems:
* A test cannot be run by itself
* A test class cannot be run by itself
* A test passes because of some previously leaked state and not because the test is actually testing the correct thing
* etc.

Reducing state leaking reduces fragility, increases confidence that tests are testing what they should be testing, and is a likely prerequisite for future parallel test running.

This ticket is for sharing a grab-bag of unrelated test fixes we worked on during WCUS.

Improve the Custom Fields meta box editing flow in the post editor
_description:
The Custom Fields meta box in the post editor still uses an older table-style editing flow. Adding, updating, and deleting fields works, but the interaction is difficult to scan and relies on color-flash feedback after AJAX actions.

This ticket proposes improving the existing Custom Fields meta box while preserving the existing custom field form contracts as much as possible.

The initial patch/prototype:
- Keeps the existing Custom Fields meta box and AJAX behavior.
- Preserves existing field names, IDs, nonces, and `data-wp-lists` behavior for add/update/delete actions.
- Shows visible success notices inside the Custom Fields meta box after adding, updating, or deleting a field.
- Removes the yellow/red row highlight animations used by `wpList` and replaces them with clearer notice feedback.
- Improves the add-new flow:
  - If there are no saved custom fields, the new-field form is shown.
  - If saved custom fields exist, the new-field form is collapsed behind an “Add custom field” button.
  - “Enter new” toggles the name control from the existing select to a text input.
  - “Cancel” clears/collapses the pending new-field form.
  - Attempting to save without selecting or entering a field name keeps the form open.
- Adjusts spacing and field layout to make saved and pending custom fields easier to scan.

The patch is intended as a starting point for design, accessibility, and backwards-compatibility feedback. In particular, review is requested on:
- Whether the add-new flow should be changed in this way.
- Whether the in-metabox notice is the right feedback pattern for add, update, and delete actions.
- Whether the visual layout changes are acceptable for this legacy admin UI.
- Whether the shared behavior between the classic editor and block-editor metabox area should be refactored further before commit.

summary: Toolbar: same W and site name behavior in the admin, the editors and the front end
_description:
This ticket proposes two fixed links in the Toolbar. The W always goes to the Dashboard. The site name always goes to the site. Both work the same in the admin, in the editors and on the front end.

It replaces #66235, which covered only the site name.

== Current behavior ==

The W and the site name are the first two items of the Toolbar.

 * A click on the W goes to the About WordPress page. It is the first item of the Toolbar, and it goes to a page people rarely need.
 * A click on the site name changes with the place. In the admin it goes to the site. On the front end it goes to the Dashboard.
 * The site name menu also changes. In the admin it has only Visit Site. On the front end it has Dashboard, Plugins and Themes.
 * When the site has no site icon, the icon changes too. It is a house in the admin and a gauge on the front end.

Since 7.1 the Toolbar is also displayed in the editors. There, the Toolbar has no link to the Dashboard. The W goes to the About page and the site name goes to the site.

== Proposal ==

'''The W'''

 * Click: the W always goes to the Dashboard.
 * Menu: Dashboard is the first item. The other items stay the same.
 * Small screens: the W stays visible. Today it is hidden under 600px.

[[Image(toolbar-w-menu.png)]]

'''The site name'''

 * Click: the site name always goes to the site.
 * Menu: the same items everywhere. Visit Site, Plugins and Themes. On multisite, Manage Site comes right after Visit Site.
 * Icon: the site icon when the site has one, as it works since 7.1. When the site has no site icon, the same default icon everywhere.

[[Image(toolbar-site-name-menu.png)]]

The Dashboard has one place, under the W. It leaves the site name menu.

Small screens:

[[Image(toolbar-small-screens.png)]]

== Why ==

 * The W gets a useful click. The logo in the top left corner is the most visible item of the Toolbar. I believe people expect it to go to the home of the admin. About WordPress is still in the menu, one click away.
 * The W menu keeps its role. It still holds the links about WordPress. Only the click changes.
 * One click to the Dashboard from everywhere. This matters most in the editors, where the Toolbar has no way back to the Dashboard today.
 * One behavior to learn. Each item does one thing. People don't need to check where they are before they click.
 * Two clear places. The W is the admin and the site name is the site. Today one item switches between both.
 * It works on multisite. My Sites stays next to the W, as today. In the Network Admin, the W goes to the network Dashboard.
 * **Better on touch screens**. A tap on the site name opens the menu. Today, in the admin, that menu has a single item.

== Accessibility ==

 * The accessible name of the W becomes "Dashboard". Today it is "About WordPress". The name says where the link goes.
 * Keyboard and focus behavior does not change.
 * Both menus have the same items in the same order everywhere. It is more predictable for screen reader users.
 * The site icon is decorative. The site name stays next to it.

== Backward compatibility ==

 * Two clicks change. The W goes to the Dashboard and not to the About page. On the front end, the site name goes to the site and not to the Dashboard.
 * The Dashboard item moves from the site name menu to the W menu. It keeps its ID.
 * People only see the items they have access to, same as today.
 * Classic themes keep their extra items (Widgets, Menus, Background and Header) after Themes.
 * The other menu items keep their IDs. Plugins that add items to these menus keep working.
 * Under 600px the Toolbar gets one more item, the W.

== Related ==

 * #66235 is the first version of this proposal, only for the site name. I will close it in favor of this ticket.
 * #28398 and #19184 asked for fixed links years ago and were closed. Since then, the site name got the site icon and the Toolbar is displayed in the editors.
 * #65088 site icon in the Toolbar.
 * #65091 Toolbar in the Site Editor and Block Editor.

summary: Tests: Let WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase reflect read-only routes
_description:
Follow-up to #40538, splitting out the structural half so it can land on its own.

== The problem ==

`WP_Test_REST_Controller_Testcase` declares nine abstract methods (`tests/phpunit/includes/testcase-rest-controller.php`, lines 24–40 on trunk today):

{{{
test_register_routes()   test_context_param()    test_get_items()
test_get_item()          test_create_item()      test_update_item()
test_delete_item()       test_prepare_item()     test_get_item_schema()
}}}

Every controller test must implement all nine. A read-only controller has no create, update or delete route, so those three methods have nothing to assert. Since [53921] and [54058] the accepted way out has been `@doesNotPerformAssertions`, with the note that it "can be reconsidered in the future".

That has not stayed flat. Trunk today carries 101 `@doesNotPerformAssertions` annotations in 26 files, and 98 of them are REST controller tests. Twenty files sit under `tests/phpunit/tests/rest-api/`, plus three under `fonts/font-library/`, two under `icons/`, and one unrelated case in `user/passwordHash.php`. Each new read-only controller inherits the pattern on the day it is written.

== Options ==

 1. '''Default implementations that assert the negative.''' Make the six operation methods non-abstract, with a default that dispatches the operation against the controller's collection and item routes and asserts it is rejected (`rest_no_route`, or the controller's documented error). A controller that supports the operation overrides the method as today. This turns 98 no-ops into real assertions with one change and no per-file work, and it stops the count growing.
 2. '''A read-only base class.''' A second testcase with the read-side methods only, and controllers pick the one that fits. Cleaner signature, but every existing read-only controller test has to move, and nothing stops a future controller extending the wrong one.
 3. '''Leave the abstract alone''' and keep annotating. The status quo.

Option 1 seems the best trade, but the default needs care: some controllers register a route and reject the method with 403 or 405 rather than `rest_no_route`, and the schema for a POST body differs per controller. A first patch could dispatch and accept any error response, then tighten.

Once the base class change lands, the remaining annotations outside the abstract methods are a per-case read, which stays on #40538.

Related: #40538, #41463, #55652, [53921], [54058].

summary: Plugin update via modal does not update plugins list until page reload
_description:
If you visit the "Plugins" page in the admin section and there is a plugin update available, the following text will be displayed:

  There is a new version of [the plugin's name] available. View version [the plugin's latest version] details or update now.

If you click the "View version ... details" link, a modal dialog box (using an iframe) will be displayed with a button to perform the update.

Before WordPress 6.5, this button was labeled "Install Update Now".  If you clicked the button, the modal would close, the text on the main page would change to "Updating..." and then finally this text would change to "Updated!" when the update was completed.

In WordPress 6.5 and later, the button is labeled "Update Now" (and has a different appearance).  If you click the button, the modal does not close, but the text on the button changes to "Updating..." and then finally "Updated!"  If you close the modal, you will see that the main page has not changed at all: the plugin still displays the old version with the same "There is a new version of [the plugin's name] available..." text.  You have to manually reload the page in order to see that the plugin has been updated to the new version.

Is this behavior intentional?  Probably the change in the button label and appearance was intentional (but that's not very important).  Keeping the modal open during the update might be intentional (although I preferred the old behavior).  But failing to update the main page seems like a bug, or at least a significant regression in functionality compared to earlier versions.

summary: Hoist strlen() out of the class_list() loop condition
WP_Http_Cookie accepts cookies with an empty or missing name
_description:
When a `WP_Http_Cookie` is created from a header string, an empty or missing name is not treated as invalid:

 * `=abc; path=/` results in `name = ''` and `value = 'abc'`. `test()` only checks for a `null` name, so it returns `true`, and `getHeaderValue()` returns `=abc`.
 * A pair without `=` (e.g. `novalue`) results in `name = ''` and `value = 'ovalue'`: `strpos()` returns `false`, so the first character of the value is cut off.
 * An array with `'name' => ''` behaves the same way.

RFC 6265 (section 5.2) says to ignore a cookie with an empty name or without `=`. The newer RFC 6265bis draft keeps such cookies, but treats `novalue` as an empty name with the value `novalue`. Either way, `ovalue` is wrong.

This came up in review of [https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/pull/13983 PR 13983] (PHPStan, #65817). That PR makes `WP_Http::normalize_cookies()` skip cookies without a name, without a value, or with a non-scalar value, so they are no longer sent through Requests. `WP_Http::buildCookieHeader()`, which is still used by `WP_Http_Curl` and `WP_Http_Streams`, can still send `=abc`.

Leaving `name` as `null` in the constructor for these cases would treat them as invalid without throwing an exception.

Related: #12761 (whitespace-only cookie pairs in the same parsing code).

summary: Editor: Add a background clip block support to facilitate text gradients
_description:
Backport of Gutenberg PR https://github.com/WordPress/gutenberg/pull/77141.

Adds a `background.backgroundClip` block support, so a block can set which box its background is painted into: `border-box`, `padding-box`, `content-box`, or the `text` itself. Clipping to the text is what gives blocks a gradient text fill, since CSS has no gradient colour.

For the text value the style engine also emits `-webkit-background-clip` and
`-webkit-text-fill-color`, and the block skips the `has-background` class because
nothing paints the block's background. For the box values only the fill colour
is reset, because `-webkit-background-clip` is an alias of `background-clip` in
Chromium and resetting it would discard the value.

The setting is not part of appearance tools. A theme opts in by setting
`settings.background.backgroundClip`, either true or an array of the values it
wants to offer.

The editor controls and the `core/heading` and `core/paragraph` opt-ins arrive with
the next Gutenberg package update.

summary: Improve the admin notices accessibility
_description:
Follow-up to #47656. See also #50442/

The admin notices accessibility has room for improvements.

Currently, all the admin notices are just text printed out on the admin pages. They have no special semantics. There are no mechanisms to inform users some important information is printed on the page other than visuals. There are no methods to navigate directly to admin notices nor established standards on their placement.

This way, users with accessibility needs will likely miss important information, as they may have no clue whether and where these messages are printed out.

Depending whether the admin notices are PHP-generated notices that appear after a page load or JavaScript-generated ones that are "injected" into the DOM, there are ways to improve their accessibility. At the very least, the following improvements should be considered, some of them were mentioned in #47656.


== All notices
- establish standards for the admin notices placement in the page: there should be one, well defined, area where notices are printed out (recommended: after the main H1)
- establish standards for the admin notices content: see the discussion related to the "text prefix" on #47656 and #50442
- the above item should apply to the whole WordPress UI, including the block editor
- "inline" notices (the ones printed out in the middle of the page): make a decision whether to keep them or allow only notices at the top of the page 
- if "inline" notices are kept, explore ways to make them more accessible
- worth considering admin notice should be visually prominent and appear within the initial viewport anyways
- consider the introduction of a dedicated PHP class with methods to get / print admin notices and additional features, also keeping into consideration [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2019/08/05/feature-project-proposal-wp-notify/ the WP Notify project] and the recent [https://make.wordpress.org/core/2020/06/15/call-for-feedback-wp-notify-v1-requirements-document/ call for feedback on the WP Notify v1 requirements document]

== PHP notices
- prepend to the document title a short text to inform users there are notices and their number: the document title is the first thing screen readers announce after a page load
- the notices should be printed out after the main H1 heading as that's the part of the content with higher chances to be navigated to
- define the page area where notices are printed out with an ARIA role that's also a landmark role, e.g. `complementary` (an `<aside>` element) or other role that is a landmark
- add a new "skip link" after the "Skip to main content" one to allow all keyboard users to jump to the notices area: this skip link should only be printed out when there are notices

== JavaScript notices
- all notices injected in the DOM should have an ARIA role `alert` or `status` depending on their "politeness" level, so that they're automatically announced by screen readers

Any additional suggestion and/or technique to improve the admin notices accessibility is very welcome.

Opening this issue for further discussion and work.

summary: Make all admin notices render after the main H1 heading
_description:
Related: #50486 / [64282]

Many important admin notices (see a few examples in the attached screenshot) render before the page main H1 heading.

I do realize they are rendered at the very top of the page to be visually prominent. However, this has a few important disadvantages:

- These notices may be entirely missed by screen reader users, as they come after the main H1 heading. Many users may jump directly to the H1 and miss anything that comes before it.
- It's not a case that an important accessibility best practice requires the main H1 heading to be the very first thing inside the `<main>` element.
- These notices aren't moved to the `<aside>` element added in #50486. As such, they are separated from other notices and aren't included in an ARIA landmark.

Basically, to my understanding, all the notices hooked to:

- network_admin_notices
- user_admin_notices
- admin_notices
- all_admin_notices

stay before the main H1 heading ''if'' they use the additional CSS class `inline`.

It is worth reminding that the admin notices that ''do not'' use the `inline` CSS class are moved via Javascript ''after'' the H1.

I'd like to propose to remove the `inline` CSS class from all these notices.

Visual prominence can be achieved by other means, for example with a good usage of white space.

This proposal is not related to 'inline' notices that are ''intentionally'' rendered in the middle of the page.

summary: Improve the focus state in the admin bar
_description:
The default focus state in the admin bar is very subtle. It's visually very similar to the focus state used for submenus in the side menu.

As indicated by #64859, this state makes the user experience somewhat confusing. In my opinion, this confusion is caused mostly because the focus state is different from other top level contexts, and doesn't clearly convey what is actually going on. 

The focus state in the adminbar should be made stronger - either by using the same focus state used in the side menu (inverted colors in blue/white) or by using the same focus state used in the main content area (outlined).

Given the context, the inverted colors makes more sense.

summary: Make the focus style consistent in Core and the Editor
_description:
Follow-up to #65645


Make sure the focus style is always at least 2 CSS pixels for both Core and the Editor.

With a few exceptions, the focus style in WordPress is provided by the means of an 'outline' around the focusable element. Actually, it's a box-shadow and for Windows High Contrast Mode there is a transparent outline in place.

For more details, please refer to #65645 where it is explained the focus box-shadow is now standardized to a CSS variable that uses a media query to detect the Device Pixel Ratio.

Right now, the thickness of this 'outline' is largely inconsistent between Core and the Editor.


The root cause is that in Core ''most'' of the focusable elements use also a border. On focus, the border changes color and the 'outline' appears. The visual thickness of this shape is thicker than the one in the Editor.

Focusable elements that don't use a border color change get a thinner focus style instead. This happens both in Core, for non-standard elements that have no border, and mor importantly in the Editor, which doesn't use a border color change.

This inconsistency is visible basically everywhere. See a few examples in the screenshots below.

For accessibility, a custom focus style should never be 'pejorative' compared to the browser native focus style. Modern browsers use a native focus style with a 2 pixels shape. See last screenshot. Note: when measuring a native focus style in the browser devtools, don't trust the devtools. Instead, measure the pixels on the screen.

summary: Remove widget accessibility mode
_description:
With the introduction of the new block editing experience for widgets management, WordPress will have four separate interfaces for managing widgets: block editing, customizer, classic widgets, and accessbility mode.

The accessibility team would like to explore merging the characteristics that accessibility mode uses for better accessibility into the classic widget screen, to cut down to only three modes of operation for widgets.

This will require identifying the characteristics of accessibility mode and finding ways to reproduce those characteristics within the existing widget UI.

The key differences that are obvious are:

1) Use of a text link to 'Add' or 'Edit'
2) Links target each widget via a URL to manage independently.
3) Selection options to choose which sidebar and position will be used for a widget.

These characteristics allow a single widget to be edited in isolation, the ability to assign a location without drag and drop, and visible text tools for handling widgets. 

One possibility to explore is having an add/edit option that opens a given widget in a modal that includes the location selection tools provided in accessibility mode.

summary: Site Icon in Settings > General: exact 512×512 image skips the crop step, so site icon sizes (32/180/192/270) are never generated
_description:
When a Site Icon is set from '''Settings > General''' using an image that is exactly 512×512, the media frame skips the crop step and saves the original attachment as `site_icon`. The crop step is what generates the site icon sizes (`site_icon-32`, `-180`, `-192`, `-270`), so they are never created.

`wp_site_icon()` then falls back to the closest registered size for every favicon tag, and browsers download a larger image than needed (e.g. a 150px–300px image for the 32×32 favicon).

The Customizer (Site Identity) does not have this problem. For an exact 512×512 image it still sends the image through `crop-image` with `context: 'site-icon'`, which creates the `cropped-` attachment with all site icon sizes. The two UIs give different results for the same image.

This has been the behaviour since the Site Icon setting was added to Settings > General in 6.5 (#54370). It is still present in trunk.

== Steps to reproduce ==

 1. On a fresh install, go to Settings > General.
 2. Click "Choose a Site Icon" and upload/select a PNG that is exactly 512×512.
 3. Note that no cropper appears. Save Changes.
 4. Inspect the attachment and the icon URLs:
{{{
wp post meta get $(wp option get site_icon) _wp_attachment_metadata --format=json
wp eval 'foreach ( array( 32, 180, 192, 270, 512 ) as $s ) { echo $s, ": ", get_site_icon_url( $s ), PHP_EOL; }'
}}}
 5. Repeat with a square image of any other size (e.g. 1024×1024). The cropper appears, and after cropping the `site_icon-*` sizes exist.

== Expected result ==

The site icon attachment has the 32, 180, 192 and 270 sizes, and `get_site_icon_url( 32 )` returns a 32×32 file, matching what happens in the Customizer or with any non-512 image.

== Actual result ==

The attachment has only the standard intermediate sizes (thumbnail/medium). `get_site_icon_url()` returns the nearest larger size for every requested size, e.g.:
{{{
32:  .../icon-150x150.png
180: .../icon-300x300.png
192: .../icon-300x300.png
270: .../icon-300x300.png
512: .../icon.png
}}}
`_wp_attachment_context` is not set to `site-icon`.

== Cause ==

`site-icon.js`, `select` handler ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/js/_enqueues/admin/site-icon.js#L118-L134 L118–134]): if the selected image already matches the required size, it calls `switchToUpdate()` and sets the hidden field to the original attachment ID, skipping the cropper entirely.

The site icon sizes are only added in `wp_ajax_crop_image()` for the `site-icon` context, via `WP_Site_Icon::additional_sizes()` on `intermediate_image_sizes_advanced` ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/wp-admin/includes/ajax-actions.php#L4092-L4119 ajax-actions.php L4092–4119]).

For comparison, the Customizer's `SiteIconControl.onSelect()` handles the exact-size case by still calling `crop-image` with a full-image crop ([https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/33ffa46a017c255cf86ac143b3f14706e0022d4d/src/js/_enqueues/wp/customize/controls.js#L4874-L4900 controls.js L4874–4900]).


== Possible fixes ==

 * Match the Customizer: in `site-icon.js`, when the image is already 512×512, call `wp.ajax.post( 'crop-image', { context: 'site-icon', cropDetails: { x1: 0, y1: 0, width: 512, height: 512, dst_width: 512, dst_height: 512 } } )` instead of using the original attachment. This keeps the existing "cropped-" duplicate behaviour discussed in #33011 / #38530.
 * Or, generate the site icon sizes on the selected attachment without creating a duplicate (e.g. when the `site_icon` option is saved), so both UIs produce the same result.

== Related ==

#54370, #33011, #38530, #36441, #58137

Category Search Fails When Search Term Contains an Ampersand Followed by a Space, Admin Page/Post Editor
_description:
Bug Report: 

Product: WordPress  
Version: 7.1.2, 7.1.3 and others  
Component: Posts / Categories / Editor  
Issue Type: Bug

**Summary**

When adding or editing a post in the WordPress admin dashboard, searching for a category whose name contains an ampersand (`&`) followed by a space does not return the expected search result.

For example, a category named **“Tour & Travel”** cannot be found when searching for `Tour & ` (including the trailing space).

2. Navigate to **Posts → Add New** or edit an existing post.
3. Open the Categories panel in the post editor.
4. Search for `Tour & `, including the space after the ampersand.
5. Observe the search results.

## Expected Behavior

The category **“Tour & Travel”** should appear in the search results when searching for `Tour & `, since the entered text matches the beginning of the category name.

## Actual Behavior

The category does not appear in the search results when the search term contains an ampersand followed by a space.

## Additional Information

- The issue occurs in the WordPress admin post editor while adding or editing a post.
- The affected category contains an ampersand followed by a space in its name.
- The issue appears to involve partial category-name matching when special characters and whitespace are present.

**Suggested investigation:** Check how the category search filters and processes search terms containing ampersands and trailing whitespace, including any differences in query tokenization or sanitization.

## Impact

This behavior makes it harder for users to find and assign categories containing ampersands when searching by partial category name.

summary: Integrate WordPress.org closed, suspended, and outdated plugins and themes API data into Core
_description:
WordPress.org Meta Trac ticket [#8447](https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8447) and WordPress.org PR [#1004](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/1004) updated the WordPress.org Plugin and Theme APIs to expose structured metadata when plugins or themes are:

1. **Closed / Removed / Suspended:** (`closed => true`, `status => 'closed'|'disabled'|'suspend'`, `closed_date`, `reason`, `reason_text`, `is_security => true|false`).
2. **Outdated / Abandoned:** (`is_outdated => true`, `outdated_notice => string`, tested beyond the last three major WordPress versions or not modified for more than two years).
3. **Inaccessible for Security Reasons:** (`is_security => true` or `reason => 'security-issue'`).

Currently, WordPress Core lacks visibility into this metadata. Site administrators may be unaware when an installed plugin or theme has been removed from the repository due to a critical security issue, closed at the author's request, or abandoned without updates. Furthermore, opening the details modal for a closed item triggers a generic `plugins_api_failed` error (`"An unexpected error occurred..."`) instead of explaining why the item is unavailable.

== Related Links & Prior Art

* **Meta Trac Ticket:** https://meta.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/8447
* **WordPress.org Pull Request:** https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/1004


----


== Proposed Solution & Changes

This patch adds complete Core support for storing, displaying, and alerting administrators about closed, suspended, outdated, or security-withdrawn plugins and themes.

=== 1. Update Check & Transient Storage

**`wp-includes/update.php`**

* In `wp_update_plugins()`:

  * Preserve `closed`, `closed_date`, `closed_reason`, `reason`, `reason_text`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, and `outdated_notice` in both the `response` and `no_update` arrays of the `update_plugins` transient.
  * Populate standalone `closed` response items into `no_update`.

* In `wp_update_themes()`:

  * Preserve `closed`, `status`, `is_closed`, `is_suspended`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, `outdated_notice`, `closed_date`, and `reason` metadata in both the `response` and `no_update` arrays of the `update_themes` transient.

=== 2. Plugins List Table UI & Inline Notices

**`wp-admin/includes/update.php`** and **`wp-admin/includes/class-wp-plugins-list-table.php`**

* `wp_plugin_update_rows()` now processes items in `no_update` when they are flagged as closed or outdated.

* In `wp_plugin_update_row()`:

  * **Security closures** (`is_security === true` or `reason === 'security-issue'`): Displays `.notice.notice-error.inline.notice-alt` with `role="alert"`: "Warning: This plugin was closed on [Date] due to a security issue and is no longer available for download. It should be uninstalled or replaced immediately."

  * **General closures:**
Displays `.notice.notice-warning.inline.notice-alt` with `role="status"`: "Notice: This plugin was closed on [Date] ([Reason]) and is no longer available for download."

  * **Outdated plugins:**
Displays `.notice.notice-warning.inline.notice-alt` with `role="status"` and the value of `outdated_notice`.

* Status badges (`Closed (Security)`, `Closed`, and `Outdated`) are rendered alongside the plugin title, with `.screen-reader-text` accessibility announcements.

=== 3. Themes Screen UI & Preview Modal

**`wp-admin/includes/theme.php`**, **`wp-admin/themes.php`**, and **`src/js/_enqueues/wp/theme.js`**

* `wp_prepare_themes_for_js()` exports `closed`, `is_suspended`, `is_security`, `is_outdated`, `closedDate`, `closedReason`, and `outdatedNotice` to JavaScript.
* Theme card overlays and badges are rendered on both PHP non-JS cards and Underscore templates (`tmpl-theme` and `tmpl-theme-single`).
* Preview modals display prominent warning/error notices containing the closure date and reason.

=== 4. Site Health Check Integration

**`wp-admin/includes/class-wp-site-health.php`**

* Adds the `closed_plugins_and_themes` test under direct tests in `WP_Site_Health::get_tests()`.

* **Critical status:**

  * Triggered when an active plugin or active theme was closed due to a security issue (`is_security === true` or `reason === 'security-issue'`).
  * Includes direct deactivation/action links.

* **Recommended status:**

  * Triggered when an active plugin or theme is closed for non-security reasons or marked as outdated.

=== 5. API Client Handling

**`wp-admin/includes/plugin-install.php`** and **`wp-admin/includes/theme-install.php`**

* In `plugins_api()` and `themes_api()`:

  * Gracefully allow objects with `error => 'closed'` to pass through without converting them into a generic `WP_Error`.

* In `install_plugin_information()` and `install_theme_information()`:

  * Render a dedicated informational modal panel displaying the closure notice, date, reason, description, and slug instead of showing a fatal error screen.

----


== Testing Instructions

=== 1. Verify Unit Tests

Run the newly added PHPUnit test suites:

```bash
./vendor/bin/phpunit tests/phpunit/tests/plugins/closedPlugins.php
./vendor/bin/phpunit tests/phpunit/tests/theme/closedThemes.php
```

Both suites should pass with all assertions successful.

=== 2. Simulate Closed & Outdated Plugins

Filter `pre_http_request` or set the `update_plugins` site transient with:

* A plugin having:

  * `closed => true`
  * `is_security => true`
  * `closed_date => '2025-01-15'`
  * `closed_reason => 'security-issue'`

* A plugin having:

  * `closed => true`
  * `reason_text => 'Author Request'`
  * `closed_date => '2024-06-20'`

* A plugin having:

  * `is_outdated => true`

Visit `wp-admin/plugins.php` and verify that the corresponding badges are displayed next to the plugin names:

* Red: `Closed (Security)`
* Grey: `Closed`
* Yellow: `Outdated`

Also verify that the inline notice rows display the correct text, ARIA roles, and styling.

=== 3. Check Site Health

Activate a plugin marked with `is_security => true` and navigate to:

`wp-admin/site-health.php`

Verify that Site Health reports a **Critical** status issue advising immediate deactivation and deletion, and that a direct deactivation link with a valid nonce is provided.

=== 4. View Plugin & Theme Information Modals

Visit:

`wp-admin/plugin-install.php?tab=plugin-information&plugin=[closed-slug]&TB_iframe=true`

Confirm that a dedicated informational panel is displayed containing the closure date, reason, and description instead of the generic error message.

summary: WordPress Notification Center proposal
_description:
For a long time people have been suggesting / daydreaming / [https://twitter.com/Ipstenu/status/966411791134699520 wishing for] a unified notification center in WordPress. People expect it, the notification center has become a staple of almost all apps/sites that have a lot to keep track of - and WordPress definitely fits in that lineup. So there’s no reason not to add one to WordPress core too.

This ticket aims to explore the details of such an implementation. I think clear limitations, a good backwards compatibility strategy and a strong UX are key to make this work for everyone.

Key features:
- One location for all notifications.
- Easy to hook into, should work out of the box.
- Flexible enough to be useful, limited enough to not get a circus.
- Accessible from anywhere.
- Accessible in the a11y sense.

Here’s my first basic idea for notification properties, feel free to chime in:
- A text field, limited to 280 characters, the length of a tweet. Probably wouldn’t want one notification to get so long that it fills up the whole visible sidebar. Links can be added to the text to trigger actions or visit pages, same as now basically.
- A timestamp.
- An icon. Could be the plugin icon, author avatar, or something like a category/message type, like info, warning, question, error, update, stuff like that, to visually distinguish notifications quickly.
- A status, meaning read or unread basically.
- Persist/show as toast. A suggestion by Joen Asmussen. Shows the notification outside the notification center for a set amount of time in a floating div. Similar to what Android/MacOS/Windows does when a notification comes in. Maybe only WordPress itself can throw notices like that. Probably not for MVP anyway.

I created a quick interactive proof-of-concept in Sketch that you can view here.

Desktop: https://sketch.cloud/s/AZz0M/all/notification-center/desktop/play
Mobile: https://sketch.cloud/s/AZz0M/all/notification-center/iphone-8-plus/play

Riad Benguella got excited by this idea and built a basic plugin to test it in your own WordPress install. https://github.com/youknowriad/newtify, and also a previous exploration at https://wordpress.org/plugins/wp-notification-center/. Developing this as a plugin is a great way to explore the best implementation, and any help is more than welcome.

Some discussion points to get this started:
- Can we agree on a set of notification properties that provide a consistent experience and that plugin authors can be happy with?
- Which notification categories can we define, and should it only ever be possible to assign a category, or are plugin authors allowed to supply icons for their own notifications too?
- How best to approach the backwards compatibility so we don’t break (all) existing admin notices? Can some type of conversion be made?
- Is it enough to only show the notifications in the sidebar, or should there be a separate notifications page, maybe with filtering? (Probably not for MVP at least)
- Are there any essential features missing from the list?

summary: oembed_cache created in post affects the post_author on export
_description: To fix ticket #34115 we've introduced a custom type `oembed_cache` in the post table. However, once an `oembed_cache` is created the `post_author` will be the user who triggers it instead of the site owner. Because of the reason above, when you try to export the blog, it'll show up as a <wp:author> in the file which is pretty confusing. It probably makes more sense to set the `post_author` as 0 or set it to the site owner.

summary: XMLRPC method "wp.getUsers" not working correctly in Multisite
_description:
Hi,

I have been testing some functionality in our app which uses XMLRPC, and it appears that I've found a bug with how the "wp.getUsers" method works on WordPress.com blogs.

summary: No way to turn off importing alt text from image XMP metadata
_description:
This is a follow-up to issue #63895.  The fix for that issue created a new `wp_get_image_alttext()` function which parses images for XMP metadata and uses that to populate the alt text for the image.  Currently `wp_get_image_alttext()` is called unconditionally - if you don't want this functionality, there does not appear to be any way to turn it off.  You could use the `wp_read_image_metadata` filter to overwrite the alt text after `wp_get_image_alttext()` has already run, but it would be better to have a way to prevent `wp_get_image_alttext()` from running a bunch of unnecessary code in the first place.

I will submit a pull request to address this.

summary: Custom style handle attached to a custom block style is never load even if the block is in the page.
_description:
== Description

I have a custom block based theme running on WP 5.9 that declares custom styles for certain blocks via the register_block_style function, but when I specify a style_handle the style is never enqueue even though the block is present in the page content (and core block assets are only loaded when they are rendered).

script-loader.php

summary: Connectors plugin install flow does not show filesystem credentials form when FTP is required
_description:
When installing a connector plugin from Settings > Connectors on a site that requires filesystem credentials, the install attempt fails with a generic notice instead of showing the standard "Connection Information" filesystem credentials form.

The regular Plugins > Add Plugin installer shows the credentials form correctly for the same plugin in the same environment.

== Steps to Reproduce ==
1. Install WordPress 7.0-RC3.
2. Log in as an administrator.
3. Force filesystem credentials, for example by setting FS_METHOD to ftpext in wp-config.php.
4. Ensure the AI plugin is installed and active.
5. Ensure one connector provider plugin is not installed, for example ai-provider-for-anthropic.
6. Go to Settings > Connectors.
7. Click Install for Anthropic.

== Actual Results ==
The page stays on Settings > Connectors and shows a generic notice:

{{{
Failed to install plugin for Anthropic.
}}}

No filesystem credentials modal is shown.

== Expected Results ==
The Connectors install flow should surface the standard WordPress "Connection Information" modal so the administrator can enter FTP credentials, matching the behavior of Plugins > Add Plugin.

== Control Test ==
Using the same environment and the same plugin:

1. Go to Plugins > Add Plugin.
2. Search for ai-provider-for-anthropic.
3. Click Install Now.

This correctly opens the "Connection Information" dialog with Hostname, FTP Username, FTP Password, and Connection Type fields.

== Environment ==
WordPress: 7.0-RC3
AI plugin: 0.9.0
Connector tested: AI Provider for Anthropic 1.0.2
Filesystem method: ftpext
Environment: Local Docker wp-env

== Notes ==
This appears to affect the Connectors page install flow that uses the REST plugin save flow. The standard plugin installer handles the filesystem credentials case correctly, so this may need special handling in the Connectors install action.

summary: Docblock improvements for 7.2
Combining characters aren't normalized to Unicode Form C on output
_description:
The HTML produced by WordPress functions like `get_the_excerpt()` and `the_content()` doesn't perform any Unicode Normalization.

This lack of normalisation is problematic because the W3C recommends Normalization Form C - https://www.w3.org/TR/charmod-norm/

It is possible to wrap these functions - for example `normalizer_normalize( get_the_excerpt(), Normalizer::FORM_C );` - but this quickly becomes cumbersome in complex themes.

Would it make sense for WordPress to ensure that the content coming out of the post object is normalized before being returned?

**Test**

My blog post contains the text `Anaïs`. The `ï` is U+0069 LATIN SMALL LETTER I and U+0308 COMBINING DIAERESIS.

When I run the output of `the_content()` through the W3C Validator, it complains

> Warning: Text run is not in Unicode Normalization Form C. 


**Background**

There's this previous ticket which talks about normalizing in the editor and on save - #30130.

However, for anyone saving plain text / markdown this doesn't seem to work. Text is saved un-normalised.

summary: HTML API: Introduce an HTML Sanitizer implementing the HTML Sanitizer API
_description:
The HTML Sanitizer API is now part of the WHATWG HTML standard ([https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/dynamic-markup-insertion.html#html-sanitization Dynamic markup insertion, §8.6 "HTML sanitization"]): `Element.setHTML()`/`setHTMLUnsafe()`, `Document.parseHTML()`/`parseHTMLUnsafe()`, the `Sanitizer` interface, and the `SanitizerConfig` dictionary. It ships unflagged in Chrome/Edge 146+ and Firefox 148+ (no Safari support yet). Sanitization has been a long-stated goal of the HTML API project; the standardized API gives us an exact, conformance-testable specification to implement instead of inventing our own semantics. This ticket proposes `WP_HTML_Sanitizer`: a pure-PHP implementation of that specification on top of `WP_HTML_Processor`, requiring no extensions. == Approach == The sanitize operation needs no DOM and no tree mutation. It is implemented as a '''filtered re-serialization of the HTML Processor's token stream''', the same pattern as `WP_HTML_Processor::serialize()`/`normalize()`, with a keep / remove-subtree / replace-with-children decision per element and attribute filtering during emission. Because the input is parsed with the HTML API's spec-compliant parser, the sanitizer cannot disagree with a browser about where a tag begins or ends, which is the property that defeats mutation-XSS by construction. Implemented and verified against the Web Platform Tests `sanitizer-api` suite (the same conformance data browsers use): * The full `SanitizerConfig` model: namespace-qualified, case-sensitive element/attribute matching (elements default to the HTML namespace, attributes to no namespace), allow-lists, remove-lists, `replaceWithChildrenElements`, per-element attribute lists, `comments`, `dataAttributes`, and the specification's configuration-validity constraints (the browser `TypeError` cases). * The built-in '''safe baseline''': removal of `base`/`embed`/`frame`/`iframe`/`object`/`script` (HTML) and `script`/`use` (SVG), event handler content attributes, `javascript:` URLs on the built-in navigating-URL-attributes list, and the SVG `animate`/`set`/`animateTransform` `attributeName` treatment. * The built-in '''safe default configuration''' (121 elements, 58 global attributes plus per-element lists) as a generated data file. A working prototype with tests built by Fable is available for review: [https://github.com/luisherranz/wordpress-develop/pull/2 draft PR with full analysis]. The WPT corpora are vendored under `tests/phpunit/data/web-platform-tests/sanitizer-api/` following the existing precedent, and the PHPUnit suite runs: {{{ $ npm run test:php -- --group html-api-sanitizer Tests: 221, Assertions: 388, Skipped: 9. (zero failures) }}} Each of the 9 skips names the exact gap it depends on (see below). == Current limitations of the prototype == * '''Fail-closed on unsupported input.''' Inputs the HTML Processor cannot yet represent (foster parenting, complex adoption-agency cases, PLAINTEXT) make `sanitize()` return `null`, never unsafe or partial output. A browser sanitizes 100% of inputs, and some refused inputs are ordinary content (`

bold

still bold`, stray text inside tables), so this is an availability limitation, not a security one. It is resolved by the HTML Processor's outstanding tree-construction work (foster parenting; the full adoption agency algorithm, noting the AAA clones elements ''with their attributes'', so cloned nodes must surface through the token stream, cf. WPT `sanitizer-in-adoption-agency.html`). * '''BODY-context fragments only''', matching `WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()`. This covers the dominant use case (post/comment content) but not `setHTML`-on-arbitrary-element parity. `create_fragment_at_current_node()` already implements most of what is needed and is currently private. * `get()`/`getUnsafe()` (canonical configuration read-back) are not implemented yet. * A string-returning API cannot reproduce a few DOM-side behaviors (adjacent text nodes merge on re-parse; `setHTML()` on a `script` context element is a no-op). These are documented rather than replicated. == Prerequisite / related HTML API work == The prototype uses only today's public API, which forced a small amount of HTML-API-layer machinery to live inside the sanitizer. Each piece below is useful independently and would be proposed separately: 1. #64567: `get_attribute_names_with_prefix()` agreeing with enqueued updates. This also fixes a composition hazard this work surfaced: `remove_attribute( 'onclick' )` followed by the (public since 6.9) `serialize_token()` currently emits `

`; the removal is ignored and the attribute degrades to a value-less boolean, because `serialize_token()` iterates the stale name list but reads values through `get_attribute()`. 2. A filtering-capable serialization path (or a shared internal token-emission helper used by both `serialize()` and consumers), so the sanitizer does not need to mirror `serialize_token()`'s emission rules. 3. Exposing attribute namespace identity (e.g. `get_attribute_namespace()`), since sanitizer configurations match attributes by (namespace, local name) and only the display-oriented `get_qualified_attribute_name()` is public today. 4. Public arbitrary-context fragment parsing (lifting the `''`-only restriction of `create_fragment()`, plus rawtext-context tokenizer states), which unlocks `setHTML` parity and 6 of the 9 skipped tests. == Relationship to KSES == This is '''not''' a `wp_kses()` replacement and is not proposed as one. The two have opposite defaults for disallowed elements (KSES keeps their contents; the Sanitizer removes the subtree, as specified), different configuration models (KSES has CSS filtering via `safecss_filter_attr()` and a large filter ecosystem; the Sanitizer has namespaces and a standardized contract), and different output conventions (the Sanitizer normalizes like a browser; KSES preserves source form). Measured on typical post content, KSES is ~4× faster (~7.5 MB/s vs ~1.8 MB/s); the difference is the cost of spec-correct HTML parsing itself, sanitizer logic adds ~1% over a raw HTML Processor parse, so Processor optimizations flow through directly. The two can coexist, with possible convergence later once the Processor's tree-construction gaps close. == Open questions == * Error convention for invalid configurations: the prototype throws `InvalidArgumentException` (mirroring the specification's `TypeError`); alternatives are `_doing_it_wrong()` + null object, or `WP_Error`. * Whether `null`-on-unsupported-input is an acceptable public contract for a first iteration, or whether foster parenting / adoption agency support should land first. * Naming and shape: `WP_HTML_Sanitizer` with `sanitize()` / `sanitize_with_config()` vs `wp_sanitize_html()`-style wrappers; whether to expose the unsafe operation initially. * Maintenance procedure for the spec-derived data (default configuration, event handler attribute list) as the specification evolves.

summary: State Styles: Scope per-instance rules to the block's root element

Fixes per-instance state styles on blocks whose root selector starts with another block's class. List Item registers `.wp-block-list > li`, and the instance class that scopes a state rule sits on the `li` itself, so swapping the leading compound for that class produced `.wp-states-xxxx > li`, which matches nothing. A breakpoint value set on a list item was written to the stylesheet but never applied.

The fix keeps a leading compound that names a different block as an ancestor and puts the instance class on the block's own compound, giving `.wp-block-list > .wp-states-xxxx`. A leading compound followed by a `wp-block-*` class still describes a nested element, as in `.wp-block-button .wp-block-button__link`, so those selectors keep the existing behaviour.

summary: wp_set_object_terms() leaves term_order at 0 for newly added terms in sorted taxonomies when term counting is deferred
_description:
For a taxonomy registered with `'sort' => true`, `wp_set_object_terms()` is meant to store terms in the order they are passed. When term counting is deferred and a term is added to an object that already has terms, the new term is left at the column default `term_order = 0`. It then sorts ahead of the existing terms instead of after them.

The wrong value is written to `wp_term_relationships` so the order of terms is destroyed.

=== Steps to reproduce ===

Add this MU plugin to a site. It registers a sorted taxonomy and defers term counting.

{{{#!php
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Term order bug reproduction
 * Description: Registers a sorted taxonomy and defers term counting, to reproduce the `term_order` bug in `wp_set_object_terms()`.
 */

add_action(
	'init',
	static function () {
		register_taxonomy(
			'byline',
			'post',
			array(
				'label'        => 'Byline Author',
				'sort'         => true,
				'args'         => array( 'orderby' => 'term_order' ),
				'show_in_rest' => true,
			)
		);

		wp_defer_term_counting( true );
	}
);
}}}

Then, in wp-admin:

   1. Go to Posts > Byline Author and create three terms: `Alice`, `Bob` and `Charlie`.
   2. Create a new post.
   3. From the Quick Edit panel, add `Alice`, then `Bob` to Byline Authors and save the post.
   4. Add `Charlie` in the same panel, after `Bob`. Save the post again.
   5. Check the Byline Authors again from the Quick Edit Panel

Result: `Chalie, Alice, Bob`

Expected: `Alice, Bob, Charlie`

See Video: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9c91783e-ecd6-4201-84de-e99e2bf08819

For sorted taxonomies, `wp_set_object_terms()` reads the object's terms again before it assigns `term_order`, and only numbers the terms it finds in that read.

That read is cached. Normally the term count update clears the cache before the read happens. When term counting is deferred, nothing clears it, so the read returns the old list without the newly added term. The new term is skipped and keeps `term_order = 0`.

`wp_set_object_terms()` does clear the cache itself, but only after this read. That was added in #40306.

We hit this during a bulk content migration. We turned off term counting for the whole run with `wp_defer_term_counting( true )` to improve migration speed. Byline authors were stored in a sorted taxonomy, and on posts with more than one author the byline order came out wrong.

summary: Name the item, or give a count, in the plugin/theme auto-update email subject lines
_description:
Follow-up of #50268, where the current subject lines were introduced in 5.5.

The subject line of the plugin/theme auto-update email is the same regardless of how many items were updated, and never says which ones. Plugins release independently of one another, so a run that has anything to do usually has a single plugin to do it for. Among the 100 most popular plugins in the directory, the median gap between releases is around 50 days, and their most recent releases fall on 40 different days. The update check runs twice a day. So the site admin sees, over and over:

{{{
[My Site] Some plugins were automatically updated
}}}

for a body that reads:

{{{
These plugins are now up to date:
- Jetpack (from version 16.1.2 to 16.1.3) : https://wordpress.org/plugins/jetpack/
}}}

The subject carries none of the information the admin actually wants, so every one of these emails has to be opened before it can be triaged or filed. Someone running a handful of sites receives a stream of identical subjects and has no way to tell, from the inbox, which one is worth a look.

== Proposal ==

When a single item of a single type was updated, name it in the subject. Otherwise, give a count instead of the word "Some".

So the two most common emails become:

{{{
[My Site] Jetpack was automatically updated
[My Site] 3 plugins were automatically updated
}}}

Plugin and theme names are not bounded in length, and some run well past what a mail client shows. A name that long should be truncated before it goes in the subject, around 40 characters with an ellipsis.

'''Success emails''' (subject built from `$successful_updates`):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins were automatically updated` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$s was automatically updated` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes were automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes were automatically updated` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have automatically updated` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes were automatically updated` ||

'''Failure and mixed emails''' (subject built from `$failed_updates`, as it is today):

|| '''Case''' || '''Current''' || '''Proposed''' ||
|| 1 plugin || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N plugins || `[%s] Some plugins have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins have failed to update` ||
|| 1 theme || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$s failed to update` ||
|| N themes || `[%s] Some themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d themes have failed to update` ||
|| plugins + themes || `[%s] Some plugins and themes have failed to update` || `[%1$s] %2$d plugins and %3$d themes have failed to update` ||

The email body is unchanged in every case.

Sites can already do all of this through the `auto_plugin_theme_update_email` filter, but the default is what the great majority of admins actually receive, and the information is right there when the subject is built.

Related: #50268, #50350, #51695, #53049

summary: Introduce WHATWG-compliant encoding name canonicalization.
_description:
WordPress largely treats character encoding names in an agnostic fashion, passing them off to browsers, `iconv()`, and `mb_convert_encoding()` transparently. This can lead to confusing data flow for text data, particularly because it’s unclear how arbitrary text coming into WordPress will be handled.

The [https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/ ENCODING spec] defines which character encodings should be supported by web-integrating systems and which variations of each encoding’s name should be treated as equivalent aliases.

For example, while `l1` and `us-ascii` are both treated by browsers as `windows-1252`, they are never recognized as such within WordPress. In fact, since `mb_convert_encoding()` and `iconv()` don’t follow this interoperability standard, they fail for a number of supported encodings.

As WordPress moves towards deprecating non-UTF-8 support (#62172), it should provide robust mechanisms for converting text at the boundaries of input and output to aid this transition.

Prior work normalized UTF-8 detection in #61182, but focused on the detection of `UTF-8` specifically, and without taking into account the additional encodings in the WHATWG standard.

Further work should provide standards-compliant canonicalization while being explicit which set of supported charsets is being detected. For instance, the set of `mysql` charset names is disjoint from the set of web standard charset names.

=== Activities requiring ENCODING support.

 - Decoding full HTML documents.
 - Reading and writing emails.
 - Printing `<meta charset>` tags.
 - Inferring MIME content type.

== Related work

 - #64427 inferring MIME content type.

summary: Add a plugin compatibility testing workflow to catch fatals with popular plugins before release
_description:
''Claude drafted this ticket, prompted and edited by me:''

WordPress 7.1 shipped and sites running WP Rocket began fataling on every request - `Uncaught TypeError: substr(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, int given in Cloudflare.php:562`. Austin Ginder reported all of his customer sites went offline until he manually patched the plugin: https://x.com/austinginder/status/2090199834787541074

Core's CI is thorough about testing core itself - PHPUnit, e2e, install and upgrade paths - but nothing currently checks that a new version of WordPress can boot with popular plugins active. That check happens informally through beta testers, hosts, and plugin authors, and this incident shows the gap: a fatal on every request, on a top-tier plugin, made it through a full release cycle.

== Proposed approach ==

Add a GitHub Actions workflow (following the structure of the existing Installation Tests and Upgrade Tests workflows) that:

 * Fetches the current top 100 plugins by popularity from the WordPress.org plugins API at run time, so there is no hardcoded list to go stale.
 * Installs WordPress via WP-CLI at the version under test (`latest`, `nightly`, or a specific version, selectable via `workflow_dispatch` so release leads can point it at a beta or RC).
 * Installs and activates each plugin one at a time, in isolation, and verifies WordPress still runs: activation exit code, a WP-CLI load check, and front end / admin requests asserting no 5xx responses and no fatals in the debug log.
 * Reports a per-plugin pass/fail table in the workflow summary, tests all plugins even when one fails, and fails the run if any plugin fatals.
 * Runs weekly against nightly on a schedule, plus on demand.

To start this would be signal-only (scheduled and manual runs with Slack notifications on failure) rather than blocking - a broken third-party plugin should not turn core CI red on every commit.

Worth noting the limits honestly: the .org API only covers free directory plugins, so this exact incident (WP Rocket is a premium plugin) would not have been caught directly - but the same class of type-change fatal could just as easily land in any of the free plugins with millions of installs, and activation smoke testing is exactly where it would surface. Testing plugins in combination, premium plugin zips, and multisite are possible follow-ups.

Full acceptance criteria and an implementation plan are written up here: https://github.com/adamsilverstein/wordpress-develop/issues/64

Patch incoming (draft PR being prepared, will link it here once it is up).

What do others think - is a run of the top 100 the right starting scope, and does any of this overlap with existing plugin directory infrastructure?

== AI Use ==

Description written with Claude Code; the linked PR contains Claude-written code and says so in its own AI Use section. I will review and test.

summary: Security audit for API key storage on the Connectors screen
_description:
The Connectors screen introduced in #64730 stores AI provider API keys using the WordPress options API. Several security concerns were discussed during the review that need to be verified.

=== Plaintext storage in the database

API keys for AI providers are currently stored as plaintext option values. These are sensitive credentials that, in the perfect world, should be encrypted. WordPress ships with libsodium (via `sodium_compat`), which could be used for authenticated encryption.

=== Masking bypass via `/wp-admin/options.php`

The current masking approach uses a filter on `option_{name}` to redact the key value in REST responses and on the Connectors page. However, the key is still visible in plaintext when visiting the hidden `options.php` screen in WP Admin. The masking filter is also temporarily removed when passing the key to the AI provider class for authentication, which may create additional windows of exposure.

=== Key portability concerns

As noted in review, just because a user is authorized to connect a provider on a site doesn't mean the key should be extractable. Encryption at rest (where only the site itself can decrypt for authenticated API calls) would mitigate this.

== Proposed actions

1. Evaluate using Sodium-based encryption for API key values stored in the options table.
2. Ensure masking is applied consistently across all surfaces (REST API, options.php, wp_options database queries) or that encryption makes masking less critical.
3. Document the threat model: who are we protecting against (other admins, database access, plugins reading options)?

summary: Remove the admin menu auto-fold feature & move responsive viewport trigger to 960px.
_description:
Since slightly before the dawn of time (definitely before r20749, but hard to pin down exactly when), the admin menu has automatically collapsed to a reduced width icon-only display on small viewports.

Originally, this occurred on viewports smaller than 900px; later that was expanded to be below 960px. 

When the responsive state of the admin menu was introduced in WordPress 3.8 as part of the MP6 redesign, the scope of the auto-fold behavior was limited to between 782px and 960px.

On today's devices, those widths only occur in a handful of limited scenarios: intentionally narrowed viewports, iPad Air in portrait mode, and smaller iPad Pro devices in portrait mode are the primary cases.

The collapsed menu can still be useful for some users, and this is not proposing to remove the ability to fold the menu; but the automatic folding behavior is now obsolete.

This proposal is limited to removing the behavior that automatically triggers a folded menu & to move the trigger for the responsive menu to happen at 960px.

This would help resolve issues like #46307, in that this menu would only ever appear if a user has explicitly made the choice to use it, and they would be able to change that choice if they needed clarification on a specific item in the menu.
